questions.q: Convert the infix expression "A + B * C" to postfix notation. Show the stack state after processing each token.
questions.a: Postfix: A B C * +. Stack trace: Start empty. Read A → output A. Read + → push + (stack: +). Read B → output B. Read * → precedence(*) > precedence(+) so push * (stack: + *). Read C → output C. End → pop * then + → output * +. A wrong answer like A B + C * reveals the student ignores precedence and processes left-to-right.

questions.q: Explain why the infix expression "(A + B) * C" produces a different postfix than "A + B * C" even though both have the same tokens.
questions.a: Parentheses force the addition to happen before multiplication. In "(A+B)*C", '(' is pushed, then '+', then ')': on ')', we pop '+' to output before pushing '*', giving A B + C *. In "A+B*C", '*' has higher precedence than '+', so '*' is pushed on top of '+', giving A B C * +. A student who says they are the same misunderstands that parentheses override precedence by acting as stack delimiters.

questions.q: Trace the conversion of "A ^ B ^ C" to postfix. What is the result and why does the associativity of ^ matter?
questions.a: Result: A B C ^ ^. ^ is right-associative. Trace: A→output, ^→push, B→output, ^→incoming ^ has same precedence as stack top ^, but right-associative means we do NOT pop the stack top; we push new ^ (stack: ^ ^). C→output. End→pop both ^ → output ^ ^. If student gives A B ^ C ^, they incorrectly used left-associativity (popping on equal precedence).

questions.q: Compare the stack operations for converting "A * (B + C) / D" and "A * B + C / D". Identify the step where the stack contents differ and explain why.
questions.a: First expression: after reading '(', stack has * (. Second: after reading '*', stack has *; then B output; then + pops * (precedence + < *), outputs *, pushes +. The difference occurs at the '+' token: in first, '(' blocks popping so + is pushed on top of *; in second, * is popped because + has lower precedence. A student missing this cannot handle parentheses as precedence isolators.

questions.q: A student writes Python code for infix-to-postfix but gets "A B C * +" for "A + (B * C)". They claim the parentheses are redundant. Evaluate this claim: is the output correct? Is the claim valid?
questions.a: Output is correct (same as without parentheses because * already has higher precedence than +). However, the claim "parentheses are redundant" is dangerous: in "A * (B + C)", parentheses are essential. The algorithm must still process '(' and ')' correctly (push '(', pop until '('). A student who thinks parentheses can be ignored will fail on expressions where parentheses change the order.

questions.q: Design an infix expression with three operators (+, *, ^) and parentheses that requires the stack to hold at least three operators simultaneously during conversion. Show the maximum stack depth.
questions.a: Example: "A ^ (B * C + D)". Trace: A→out, ^→push(^), (→push(^), (, *→push(^, (, *), B→out, +→pop * (precedence + < *), push + (stack: ^, (, +), C→out, )→pop +, pop ( (stack: ^), D→out, end→pop ^. Max stack depth = 3 (^, (, * then ^, (, +). A good answer demonstrates understanding of precedence, parentheses, and stack growth.
